## Results

Six rows covering the cheap operations consumers hit on every error-producing
hot path. Stdlib baselines (`errors.New`, `fmt.Errorf`) are included so the
typed-error overhead is visible directly — not hidden behind absolute numbers.

```
BenchmarkErrorsNewBaseline-8   	734859775	    0.32 ns/op	    0 B/op	0 allocs/op
BenchmarkFmtErrorfBaseline-8   	  2143618	  103.00 ns/op	   80 B/op	2 allocs/op
BenchmarkFmtErrorfRender-8     	246194562	    0.99 ns/op	    0 B/op	0 allocs/op
BenchmarkCodeOf-8              	 20175765	   12.32 ns/op	    0 B/op	0 allocs/op
BenchmarkHasCode_NoMatch-8     	 14198836	   17.06 ns/op	    0 B/op	0 allocs/op
BenchmarkPrefixMatcher-8       	 21742249	   11.08 ns/op	    0 B/op	0 allocs/op
```

## How to read this

- **`errors.New` baseline** is the floor — the SDK's typed error API will never beat the stdlib's "store a string" sentinel.
- **`fmt.Errorf` baseline** is the more honest comparison point: any typed-error library has to do the same job (build + wrap), so 103 ns/op + 80 B + 2 allocs is what we're up against.
- **`CodeOf` / `HasCode` / `PrefixMatcher`** are the introspection paths consumers hit on the hot side (routers, sinks, retry deciders). Zero allocations and ~10-17 ns/op — these stay cheap even at high error rates.
- **`FmtErrorfRender`** is included to show that rendering a wrapped error is essentially free; the construction cost dominates.

## Methodology

- `cd pkg/v1 && go test -run '^$' -bench=. -benchmem -benchtime=200ms ./errs`
- Bench output captured verbatim into this file.
- Single run, no `benchstat -count=5` variance indicator yet — numbers should be treated as ±10%.
